Today it's her skills in business which have expanded the label to some 30 stores worldwide, from New York to Beijing. CNN's Andrew Stevens caught up with the designer in Hong Kong to talk about what it's like to lead both the business and creative direction of a global fashion line. Tam: The business side is like designing, it's like I like the touch of the fabric, I like to know the details about it. And you feel about it, you know about the deal, because who's the person who knows what the best deal for you is? Yourself. It's like designing clothes, I love to know how to solve every single thing, you know. Like what kind of budget . Stevens: It's just natural curiosity? Tam: Natural curiosity, I love it. I love every aspect of it. Stevens: Who have you learned your business skills from or have you made it up as you went along? Tam: I self-taught myself in business; I know nothing about the business, I learned everything -- about the pricing, the shipping, the contracts, everything -- by doing it. When you're doing it yourself, you know everything. If you don't do it, you just listen to somebody telling you how to do it, you're not experiencing it. Once you're experiencing it, you can grow so much from it. Once you experience it, you can go further, much further. It's a feeling of it. Tam: She inspired me so much you know, like you say, the determination, persistence. When she really wanted to make something, she would really go to the end, she'd really want to make it happen and I see her, she's really the force behind me. We were quite poor, we had no money, my parents were working really hard. When I grew up, I saw them working so hard, and then deep inside myself that I wanted to change the situation, I wanted to make something, this one thing. Stevens: What do you think are the most important qualities for a businessperson? Tam: For me, it's most important, a vision, determination, and to never say no to yourself. And be open to criticisms, open to learning, and open to criticisms and knowing nothing about the business; nothing, so you can learn everything by knowing nothing, you know, and be successful in the things that you didn't know. Stevens: You work in a very creative industry, how do you keep your staff motivated in this industry, how do you keep them going, how do you keep them working for you? Tam: I always tell them my story, how I was in school when my teacher asked for one outfit -- I give them 8 outfits. I told them, do things that I didn't ask you, give me, do your work with passion, it's more important than "Oh, 6 o'clock, I have to leave." Do something that is out of the box. E-mail to a friend .

Leading fashion designer Vivienne Tam spoke with CNN’s Andrew Stevens in *The Boardroom*. Since entering the fashion business in the early 1980s and establishing her own brand in the 1990s, Tam has risen to prominence with her signature East-meets-West aesthetic. Today, it is her business expertise that has helped expand the label to some 30 stores worldwide, from New York to Beijing.

CNN’s Andrew Stevens caught up with the designer in Hong Kong to discuss what it is like to lead both the business and creative direction of a global fashion line.

**Tam:** The business side is like designing. I love the touch of the fabric; I like to understand the details. You feel it, and you understand the deal, because who knows what the best deal for you is? Yourself. It is like designing clothes: I love knowing how to solve every single thing, such as what kind of budget is needed.

**Stevens:** Is it simply natural curiosity?

**Tam:** Natural curiosity. I love it. I love every aspect of it.

**Stevens:** From whom did you learn your business skills, or did you make it up as you went along?

**Tam:** I taught myself business. I knew nothing about it, but I learned everything — pricing, shipping, contracts, everything — by doing it. When you do it yourself, you understand everything. If you do not do it and simply listen to someone telling you how it should be done, you are not truly experiencing it. Once you experience it, you can grow so much from it. Once you experience it, you can go further, much further. It is a feeling.

**Stevens:** When you won the Hong Kong Businesswoman of the Year award, you said that your mother was one of your greatest inspirations. How did she inspire you?

**Tam:** She inspired me so much — her determination, her persistence. When she really wanted to accomplish something, she would see it through to the end. She truly wanted to make things happen, and I saw that in her. She is really the force behind me. We were quite poor; we had no money, and my parents worked very hard. As I grew up, I saw how hard they worked, and deep inside I wanted to change the situation. I wanted to make something of myself.

**Stevens:** What do you think are the most important qualities for a businessperson?

**Tam:** For me, the most important qualities are vision, determination, and never saying no to yourself. You must also be open to criticism and open to learning. Even if you know nothing about business, you can learn everything from that starting point. By knowing nothing, you remain open, and you can succeed in areas that were once unfamiliar to you.

**Stevens:** You work in a very creative industry. How do you keep your staff motivated? How do you keep them going, and how do you keep them working for you?

**Tam:** I always tell them my story. When I was in school and my teacher asked for one outfit, I gave her eight. I tell them: do things I did not ask you to do. Give more. Do your work with passion. That is more important than saying, “Oh, it is six o’clock; I have to leave.” Do something out of the box.

HONG KONG, China (CNN) — Vivienne Tam is a designer whose work blends artistic imagination with strong commercial instincts, from the catwalk to retail shelves.

Prominent fashion designer Vivienne Tam appeared on CNN’s *The Boardroom* with Andrew Stevens. After entering the fashion industry in the early 1980s and launching her own label in the 1990s, Tam became well known for designs that combine Eastern and Western influences. Her business abilities have since helped grow the brand to around 30 shops internationally, including locations from New York to Beijing.

CNN’s Andrew Stevens met Tam in Hong Kong to discuss what it means to oversee both the creative and commercial sides of an international fashion business.

**Tam:** To me, business is similar to design. I enjoy feeling the fabric and understanding every detail. It is the same with a deal — you need to sense it and understand it. After all, who is best placed to know what arrangement works best for you? You are. Designing clothes is like that too. I want to understand how to work through every issue, including things like budgets.

**Stevens:** So it comes from natural curiosity?

**Tam:** Yes, natural curiosity. I enjoy it. I love every part of it.

**Stevens:** Where did you develop your business knowledge? Did someone teach you, or did you figure it out along the way?

**Tam:** I taught myself business. At first, I knew absolutely nothing about it. I learned everything by doing it — pricing, shipping, contracts, all of it. When you handle things personally, you understand them fully. If you only hear someone explain how something works, you do not truly experience it. But once you go through it yourself, you can learn and grow a great deal. That experience allows you to move ahead — much further. You develop a real feel for it.

**Stevens:** When you received the Hong Kong Businesswoman of the Year award, you said your mother was one of your biggest inspirations. In what way did she influence you?

**Tam:** She influenced me tremendously. She showed me determination and persistence. When she truly wanted to achieve something, she would keep going until the end and make it happen. I saw that in her, and she has always been a driving force behind me. We were quite poor and did not have money. My parents worked extremely hard. Growing up and watching them work so hard made me feel, deep inside, that I wanted to change our circumstances. I wanted to create something and make something happen.

**Stevens:** What qualities do you believe matter most for someone in business?

**Tam:** For me, the key qualities are having vision, being determined, and never telling yourself no. You also need to be willing to accept criticism, willing to learn, and open to feedback. Even if you know nothing about business, that can allow you to learn everything from the beginning. You can succeed in areas you once knew nothing about.

**Stevens:** Fashion is a highly creative field. How do you keep your team inspired and committed? How do you encourage them to keep working with you?

**Tam:** I often share my own story with them. When I was in school and my teacher asked for one outfit, I created eight. I tell my staff to do more than what I ask, to bring extra ideas, and to approach their work with passion. That matters more than thinking, “It’s 6 o’clock, so I have to leave.” I encourage them to think beyond the usual limits.

Below is a **fictional, CNN-inspired news-magazine transcript/article** — not an actual interview or real CNN transcript.

---

## In Hong Kong, Vivienne Tam Talks Fashion, Business, and Leading With Cultural Confidence  
**An imagined interview with Andrew Stevens**

**HONG KONG** — In a city where East meets West not as a slogan but as a daily rhythm, fashion designer **Vivienne Tam** has built a career turning cultural conversation into commercial success.

Known for blending Chinese heritage with contemporary global design, Tam has long occupied a distinctive space in fashion: part entrepreneur, part artist, part cultural ambassador. From her early international breakthrough to her continued evolution in a changing luxury market, Tam’s work reflects a central belief — that creativity and business are not opposing forces, but partners.

In this imagined conversation in Hong Kong, **Andrew Stevens** sits down with Tam to discuss business instincts, creative direction, inspiration, and leadership.

---

### Transcript

**ANDREW STEVENS:**  
Vivienne Tam, thank you for joining us here in Hong Kong.

**VIVIENNE TAM:**  
Thank you. It’s wonderful to be here. Hong Kong has always been such an important place for me — full of energy, contrast, and possibility.

**STEVENS:**  
You’ve built a global fashion brand with a very recognizable identity. Many designers are strong creatively, but the business side can be challenging. How did you develop your business instincts?

**TAM:**  
I think from the beginning I understood that fashion is not only about making beautiful clothes. It’s about communication. It’s about understanding people — how they live, what they dream about, how they want to express themselves.

Business, for me, came from listening. Listening to customers, to buyers, to the culture around me. You need creativity, but you also need discipline. You need to understand timing, production, quality, distribution. A dress is not just a dress — it has to arrive at the right moment, in the right place, with the right story.

**STEVENS:**  
So for you, commerce doesn’t dilute creativity?

**TAM:**  
No, not if you are clear about who you are. Business can actually support creativity. If the business is healthy, you have more freedom to experiment. But you have to protect your vision. You cannot follow every trend. You need to know your own language.

**STEVENS:**  
Your work often draws on Chinese culture, but it has always been presented in a very modern, international way. How do you decide what direction to take creatively?

**TAM:**  
I always start with curiosity. I may be inspired by a traditional motif, a painting, a temple carving, a street market, or even technology. But I don’t want to reproduce the past. I want to transform it.

Chinese culture is very rich — thousands of years of symbols, craftsmanship, philosophy. But culture is alive. It changes. My question is always: how does this speak to women today? How does it feel in New York, Paris, Shanghai, Hong Kong? How does tradition move forward?

**STEVENS:**  
That balance — heritage and modernity — has become much more visible in global fashion. When you began, was it more difficult to convince international audiences that this perspective belonged on the world stage?

**TAM:**  
Yes, I think so. At that time, many people had a very narrow idea of what “Chinese design” meant. Sometimes it was exoticized, sometimes it was misunderstood. I wanted to show something more personal and more contemporary.

For me, being Chinese was not a costume. It was part of my identity. But I also lived in a global world. So the work had to express both — rooted, but open.

**STEVENS:**  
Hong Kong itself has that quality — rooted, but open.

**TAM:**  
Exactly. Hong Kong is a bridge. It has speed, business energy, international thinking, but also deep cultural memory. You see old and new together everywhere. That tension is very inspiring.

**STEVENS:**  
Where do you look for inspiration now?

**TAM:**  
Everywhere. Travel, art, architecture, young people, digital culture. I’m very interested in how technology changes the way we see beauty and identity. But I’m also inspired by craftsmanship — by the human hand.

Sometimes the inspiration comes from something very simple: a color in the street, a woman’s attitude, the way someone mixes clothes unexpectedly. Fashion is about observing life.

**STEVENS:**  
The fashion industry has changed dramatically — e-commerce, social media, faster consumer cycles, sustainability pressures. How do you lead a brand through that kind of change?

**TAM:**  
You have to stay flexible but not lose your soul. The tools change. The customer changes. The speed changes. But the values of the brand must be consistent.

Leadership is about giving direction, but also creating space for others. I work with teams, and I want people to feel they can contribute ideas. Fashion is collaborative. You need strong vision, but you cannot do everything alone.

**STEVENS:**  
How would you describe your leadership philosophy?

**TAM:**  
I believe in clarity, respect, and positive energy. People do their best work when they feel trusted. But they also need to know the standard. In fashion, details matter. A seam, a color, a proportion — small things change everything.

As a leader, I try to be both demanding and encouraging. You push for excellence, but you also nurture creativity.

**STEVENS:**  
Is there a difference between being a designer and being the head of a company?

**TAM:**  
Yes. As a designer, you can focus on emotion and imagination. As the head of a company, you must think about people, budgets, strategy, timing. You have to make decisions that affect many others.

But the two roles are connected. The creative vision gives the business meaning. The business gives the creative vision structure.

**STEVENS:**  
Many young designers today want global recognition very quickly. What advice would you give them?

**TAM:**  
First, know who you are. Don’t just copy what is popular. Fashion moves very fast, but identity takes time.

Second, learn the business. Understand fabric, production, pricing, customers. Creativity is important, but if you cannot deliver, it becomes only a dream.

Third, be patient. A brand is built season by season, relationship by relationship. Success is not only one show or one viral moment. It is consistency.

**STEVENS:**  
You’ve often spoken through your designs about cultural connection. At a time when the world can feel divided, do you see fashion as a way to create dialogue?

**TAM:**  
Yes, absolutely. Fashion is visual, emotional, immediate. People may not speak the same language, but they can feel something through design.

When I bring Chinese elements into contemporary fashion, I’m not only showing decoration. I’m sharing stories — about beauty, history, humor, strength. If people become curious, if they ask questions, then fashion has opened a door.

**STEVENS:**  
What does success mean to you now?

**TAM:**  
Success is being able to continue creating with authenticity. It is seeing people wear the clothes and make them their own. It is also inspiring younger generations to feel proud of their culture and confident in the world.

**STEVENS:**  
And what still challenges you?

**TAM:**  
The challenge is always to stay fresh. You cannot repeat yourself. You must keep learning. The world changes, and you must change with it — but in a way that remains true.

**STEVENS:**  
Vivienne Tam, thank you very much.

**TAM:**  
Thank you. It was a pleasure.

---

## Analysis

Vivienne Tam’s career reflects one of the central challenges in modern fashion: how to turn a distinct creative identity into a sustainable global business.

Her approach combines cultural storytelling with commercial pragmatism. Rather than treating heritage as nostalgia, Tam frames it as a living source of innovation. And in an industry increasingly shaped by speed, digital platforms, and shifting consumer values, her emphasis on consistency and authenticity offers a counterpoint to trend-driven fashion.

For Tam, leadership appears to rest on balance: creativity with discipline, heritage with reinvention, ambition with patience. In Hong Kong — a city that mirrors many of those same contrasts — that philosophy feels particularly at home.

**News-Style Interview Transcript: Vivienne Tam on Building an East-Meets-West Fashion Brand**

**Program:** *Global Business & Style*  
**Guest:** Vivienne Tam, Fashion Designer  
**Topic:** Fashion, entrepreneurship, cultural identity, leadership  

---

**HOST:** Vivienne Tam, thank you for joining us. You’re known around the world for blending Eastern and Western influences in fashion. When you look back at your rise in the industry, what stands out most?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** Thank you for having me. What stands out is the journey of bringing my own cultural identity into a global fashion conversation. I grew up surrounded by Chinese art, symbolism, and craftsmanship, but I was also inspired by the energy of the West—especially New York, where fashion is fast, bold, and constantly changing. My rise was not overnight. It was built through persistence, curiosity, and a belief that culture can be modern, wearable, and universal.

**HOST:** Your brand is often described as “East meets West.” What does that phrase mean to you?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** For me, it is not simply putting a Chinese motif on a Western silhouette. It is about creating harmony between two worlds. It could be the philosophy behind a design, the symbolism of a pattern, or the way a garment moves. I want my clothes to feel global but still have a soul. East meets West means respecting tradition while making it relevant for today.

**HOST:** Was it difficult in the beginning to convince the fashion world that this cultural fusion could work commercially?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** Yes, of course. When you do something different, people may not immediately understand it. Some buyers want what they already know will sell. But I believed there was a customer who wanted fashion with meaning—something artistic, intelligent, and modern. Over time, people began to see that cultural storytelling could be powerful in fashion. It became part of the identity of the brand.

**HOST:** What business lessons did you learn while building Vivienne Tam as a global label?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** The first lesson is to know who you are. A brand must have a clear identity. Trends change every season, but your values should remain strong. The second lesson is to listen—to customers, to your team, to the market. Creativity is important, but business discipline is also important. You need to understand production, pricing, retail, and timing. The third lesson is resilience. There are always challenges in fashion: economic changes, competition, shifting consumer habits. You have to adapt without losing your essence.

**HOST:** Many designers struggle to balance creativity with commercial reality. How do you approach that balance?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** I think creativity and business should support each other. A beautiful idea must eventually become something people can wear and enjoy. At the same time, if you only think about business, the work can lose its emotion. I always ask: Is this design meaningful? Is it wearable? Does it represent the brand? If the answer is yes, then we can find the right way to bring it to market.

**HOST:** You’ve spoken before about the influence of your mother. How did she shape your path?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** My mother had a very strong influence on me. She taught me discipline, independence, and appreciation for craft. She was resourceful and hardworking, and she showed me that women can be strong and creative at the same time. From her, I learned the importance of patience and detail. In fashion, every stitch matters. In business, every decision matters. That mindset came from my upbringing.

**HOST:** Did she encourage you to pursue fashion?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** She encouraged me to be capable and determined. Like many mothers, she wanted security for her child, but she also understood that I had a creative spirit. Her example gave me confidence. Even when the path was uncertain, I carried her strength with me.

**HOST:** As a leader, how do you motivate your staff, especially in such a demanding industry?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** I try to motivate people by giving them purpose. Fashion can be stressful—deadlines, shows, production schedules—but when the team understands the bigger vision, they feel connected. I want them to know they are not just making clothes. They are helping tell stories, connect cultures, and create beauty.

**HOST:** What does that look like day to day?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** Communication is very important. I share ideas with the team, and I also listen to them. I encourage people to be curious and to bring new perspectives. I like a team environment where people feel respected. When people feel ownership, they do better work. I also believe in leading by example. If I am passionate, disciplined, and open-minded, that energy spreads.

**HOST:** Your work has often reflected art, technology, spirituality, and cultural symbolism. How do you keep the brand fresh after so many years?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** I stay curious. The world is always changing, and inspiration can come from anywhere—art, architecture, young people, digital culture, traditional festivals, even conversations. I don’t want the brand to be frozen in the past. Heritage is a foundation, not a limitation. The key is to keep reinterpreting it.

**HOST:** What advice would you give to young designers who want to build a brand with cultural identity?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** Be authentic. Do not use culture only as decoration. Understand it, respect it, and make it personal. Also, learn the business side. Talent is important, but a brand needs structure. You must be able to dream and execute. And finally, be patient. Success takes time.

**HOST:** When you think about your legacy, what do you hope people remember?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** I hope people remember that I helped build bridges through fashion. Clothing can be more than something beautiful—it can carry history, emotion, and connection. **Imagined Interview Transcript: Vivienne Tam on Business, Resilience, and Creative Leadership**

**Interviewer:** Vivienne, you’re known globally as a designer, but you’ve also built a major international business. Did you have formal training in business?

**Vivienne Tam:** No, I was really self-taught in business. My background was in design and creativity, not management textbooks or finance courses. When I began, I learned by doing—by making mistakes, listening to people, negotiating with factories, understanding customers, and watching how markets changed.  

In fashion, creativity is only one part of the work. You also have to understand production, timing, cash flow, distribution, and branding. I didn’t learn those things in a classroom. I learned them because I had to survive.

**Interviewer:** Was that difficult—moving from the creative side into the business side?

**Vivienne Tam:** Of course. Many creative people think business is something separate from art, but I don’t see it that way. Business can protect creativity. If you don’t understand the business, someone else controls your vision.  

For me, learning business was about learning how to keep my independence. I wanted to create designs that reflected my culture and my ideas, and I needed the structure to bring them to the world.

**Interviewer:** You were named Hong Kong Businesswoman of the Year. What did that recognition mean to you?

**Vivienne Tam:** It was very meaningful because Hong Kong is such an important part of my identity. To be recognized not only as a designer but as a businesswoman was special. It showed that creativity can be a serious business force.  

I also felt proud because it represented a journey—from very humble beginnings to being able to build something international. Awards are not the reason we work, but they can remind you that the struggles had purpose.

**Interviewer:** You’ve spoken before about growing up with very little. How did your upbringing shape you?

**Vivienne Tam:** I grew up poor, and that experience never leaves you. When you don’t have many resources, you learn to be inventive. You learn not to waste. You learn to observe carefully.  

As a child, I was surrounded by limitations, but limitations can become a kind of creative training. If you cannot buy what you want, you imagine it. If you cannot access something, you find another way. That mindset helped me later in design and business.

**Interviewer:** Did poverty make you more determined?

**Vivienne Tam:** Yes, but it also made me practical. Dreams are important, but when you come from very little, you understand that dreams must be built step by step. I learned discipline. I learned patience. I learned that you cannot wait for perfect conditions.

**Interviewer:** Many people see fashion as glamorous, but your story highlights persistence.

**Vivienne Tam:** Fashion has glamour, but behind it there is a lot of work—late nights, financial pressure, uncertainty, rejection. People see the runway, but they don’t always see the years of effort behind one collection.  

You need passion, but passion alone is not enough. You need resilience.

**Interviewer:** What advice would you give to leaders in creative industries today?

**Vivienne Tam:** First, know who you are. In creative industries, identity is everything. Trends come and go, but your point of view must be strong.  

Second, learn the business. Even if you are an artist, designer, filmmaker, or musician, understand contracts, budgets, technology, and your audience. Business knowledge gives you freedom.  

Third, respect culture, but don’t be trapped by it. I have always loved bringing East and West together, tradition and modernity together. Creativity grows when you connect worlds.

**Interviewer:** What about leading teams?

**Vivienne Tam:** A creative leader must give people space, but also direction. You cannot control every idea, but you must create a clear vision. People need to know what the brand stands for.  

Also, listen to younger generations. They see the world differently. Technology, sustainability, identity—these are all changing how creative businesses work.

**Interviewer:** How should creative leaders handle failure?

**Vivienne Tam:** Don’t be afraid of failure, but don’t ignore it either. Study it. Ask what it is teaching you. Sometimes failure means the timing was wrong. Sometimes it means the idea needs improvement. Sometimes it means you must be braver.  

In business, you cannot be too emotional about every setback. You must keep moving.

**Interviewer:** Looking back, what are you most proud of?

**Vivienne Tam:** I’m proud that I stayed true to my voice. I wanted to show that Chinese culture, Asian culture, and global culture could speak together in a modern way. I’m proud that I built a business from creativity, and that I did it as a woman from humble beginnings.  

Most of all, I’m proud that my work has connected people. Fashion is not only clothing—it is communication.

**Interviewer:** And your final message to emerging creative entrepreneurs?

**Vivienne Tam:** Believe in your vision, but be prepared to work harder than you imagine. Learn everything. Stay curious. Stay humble. And remember: creativity is powerful, but when creativity and business come together, you can build something that lasts.
